questions.question: Describe the inauguration ceremony of Nelson Mandela on 10 May 1994.
questions.answer: On 10 May 1994 at the sandstone amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria, Mandela was inaugurated as the FIRST BLACK PRESIDENT of South Africa. He took the oath of office, joined on stage by his daughter Zenani and his deputies F.W. de Klerk and Thabo Mbeki. The new South African flag was raised; the African anthem 'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika' and the old anthem were sung side by side; the South African Air Force performed a fly-past. The day formally ended three centuries of white rule and the system of apartheid.

questions.question: What does Mandela mean by 'twin obligations'? Why could a black man not fulfil them under apartheid?
questions.answer: Mandela writes that every man has TWO obligations: to his FAMILY and to his PEOPLE. In a free society, both can be fulfilled. But under apartheid, doing duty to one's people forced one into conflict with the state — at the cost of family. Children grew up without fathers (in prison or exile); fathers were stopped at the colour line. The system therefore SHATTERED ordinary lives, making both family and public duty impossible.

questions.question: Describe the contrast between the caged tiger and the wild tiger in Norris's poem.
questions.answer: CAGED — paces slowly back and forth on PADS OF VELVET behind the BARS OF HIS CAGE. He IGNORES visitors. At night, he hears the patrol car and the silence and stares at the brilliant stars longing for a freedom he cannot have. WILD — slides through LONG GRASS in his element; LURKS near a WATER-HOLE to ambush deer; or terrorises a VILLAGE by snarling near its huts. The contrast is between SLOW PACING and SWIFT MOVEMENT, BARS and OPEN GRASS, PASSIVE GAZE and ACTIVE HUNT — between CAPTIVITY and FREEDOM.

questions.question: What does Mandela mean by saying that 'the oppressor is as unfree as the oppressed'? Discuss with examples from the chapter.
questions.answer: Mandela's insight is that FREEDOM is INDIVISIBLE — where one group denies freedom to another, BOTH ARE TRAPPED. The OPPRESSED lose vote, dignity, education, freedom of movement, often family and life. But the OPPRESSOR is also a prisoner — of HATRED (which deforms his soul), of PREJUDICE (which prevents him from seeing the human in the other), and of FEAR (the constant anxiety of maintaining a system that requires force, lies and surveillance). EXAMPLES — (i) White police, judges, prison guards lived their lives within a system that treated fellow humans as less than human — a daily violence to their own conscience. (ii) The white minority lived in fear of the black majority. (iii) Mandela's reconciliation with former enemies (de Klerk became his deputy) showed that releasing the oppressed also LIBERATES the oppressor. WIDER MEANING — the free society is the one where everyone is free.

questions.question: What unifies Mandela's prose and Norris's poem as Chapter 2 of First Flight? Discuss the chapter as a meditation on freedom.
questions.answer: Both pieces explore FREEDOM from OPPOSITE poles. MANDELA from the FREEDOM SIDE — the day a long imprisonment ends; the public ceremony, the new flag, the African anthem, the tribute to comrades, the embracing of former enemies, the long walk that brought him there, the long walk still ahead. The voice is calm, public, factual. NORRIS from the CAPTIVITY SIDE — the imagined eye of a tiger pacing in a zoo, alternating with images of his lost wild life. The voice is quiet, intimate, image-based. Both ask, WHAT IS FREEDOM? Mandela answers BIG — freedom is the right of an entire people to dignity, vote, future. Norris answers SMALL — freedom is the right of a wild creature to its true environment and nature. Mandela's insight that 'the oppressor is as unfree as the oppressed' connects the two pieces — just as apartheid imprisoned both blacks and whites, the tiger's cage diminishes both keeper and kept. The chapter is therefore a study of freedom at every scale — political, personal, animal. It teaches us to value freedom and recognise its absence.
